headline: The fix that cost a nation IQ points
dek: In 1921 a chemist put lead in gasoline to stop engines knocking. More than half of Americans alive in 2015 had too much lead in their blood as small children.

slides.label: The bright idea
slides.title: Stop the knock
slides.text: Early car engines knocked: the fuel burned unevenly, wore out parts and wasted power. Fix it, and cars could be faster, stronger and cheaper to run.
slides.alt: A busy Los Angeles intersection in 1922, with streetcars, early automobiles and a Union Gasoline station
slides.credit: North Broadway and Sunset Boulevard, Los Angeles, 1922. Automobile Club of Southern California. Public domain.

slides.label: It worked
slides.title: A pinch of lead
slides.text: In 1921 Thomas Midgley found that a little tetraethyl lead in gasoline stopped the knock. It went on sale as Ethyl, and it was hailed as a triumph of chemistry.
slides.alt: A rusted red Atlantic gasoline pump with a yellow and blue Ethyl anti-knock compound emblem
slides.credit: Atlantic Ethyl pump, Leola, Pennsylvania. John Margolies, 1982. Library of Congress. Public domain.

slides.label: Wait, what?
slides.title: Sixty seconds of proof
slides.text: In October 1924, workers making the additive at a New Jersey refinery began to die. That month, Midgley poured it on his hands for reporters and breathed its vapor for a minute. The year before, he had taken time off to recover from lead poisoning.

slides.label: The backfire
slides.title: Lead in every city
slides.statLabel: IQ points lost by Americans alive in 2015, one study estimates
slides.text: For decades the lead came out of tailpipes, settled into dust and soil, and got into children, whose brains it harms.
also: Source: McFarland, Hauer and Reuben, PNAS, 2022

slides.label: Then he did it again
slides.title: A safe fridge, a hole in the sky
slides.text: In 1928 he made CFCs, sold as Freon: no fire, no poison, safe in any kitchen. They were so stable they drifted up to the stratosphere, where sunlight split them and the chlorine ate the ozone layer.
slides.alt: A NASA satellite map of the globe from below, with a large purple ozone hole covering Antarctica
slides.credit: The ozone hole over Antarctica, October 1, 1998. NASA. Public domain.

slides.label: Could anyone have seen it coming?
slides.title: The lead, yes. The ozone, no.
slides.text: Lead poisoning had been known for centuries, and the refinery deaths of 1924 made the papers. The chemistry that destroys ozone was first described in 1974, thirty years after Midgley died.

slides.label: The long cleanup
slides.title: A century to undo
slides.text: The US finished banning leaded gas for cars in 1996. The last country stopped selling it for cars in 2021. A 1987 treaty phased out CFCs, and the ozone hole over Antarctica should recover by about 2066.

slides.label: How the pattern works
slides.title: Nobody was watching the air
slides.text: Both fixes worked exactly where they were aimed: inside the engine, inside the fridge. The harm landed where nobody was measuring: in the air, on a windowsill, twenty miles up.

slides.label: How you do this
slides.title: Your fixes move problems too
slides.text: A team keeps missing deadlines, so you add a daily status meeting. Deadlines improve. Focus time disappears, and the engineers start working nights. The problem didn't go away. It moved.
also: Clutter that moves to the garage
A cost cut that lands on another team's budget

slides.label: Before your next fix
slides.title: Ask: where does it go?
slides.text: When something works, follow the problem out the door. Where does it land, who lives there, and who is watching?
